overview.title: Measure in context
overview.lead: A radiograph brings together the visual references used in planning. Measurement tools let you position points, draw lines and review measurements directly on the image.
overview.calibration: Calibration establishes the relationship between the image and a known dimension. This is the starting point for working with distances at the radiograph's scale.
overview.references: Distances, angles and circles support different ways of reading the image. Each tool builds an annotation from the points selected during your analysis.
overview.review: Keep your references visible as you review the plan. Annotations help you follow what has been measured and return to the points used in the assessment.

calibration.question: Why calibrate the image before measuring?
calibration.answer: Calibration relates a known dimension to the radiograph's scale. It provides the starting point for reading distances and dimensions on the image rather than working only with the file's pixels.

distance.question: How do I measure a distance?
distance.answer: Select the distance tool and position two points on the radiograph. A line connects the points, and you can read the distance on the image using the calibrated scale.

angle.question: How are angles represented?
angle.answer: The tool uses reference lines defined on the image to represent the angular relationship between them. The value appears in degrees alongside the annotation, so you can check the references used.

circle.question: What are circle annotations used for?
circle.answer: Circles provide references for following the shapes and dimensions of a region on the radiograph. A circular annotation complements the distance and angle tools according to what you need to examine on the image.

review.question: Can I check the points used in each measurement?
review.answer: Yes. Annotations remain visible on the radiograph so you can identify the points, lines and shapes used in the analysis. This lets you review what was measured while keeping the image's context in view.
